https://www.cei.int/ansa/178219.text: Europe's Tallest Statue of the Virgin Mary Soars Above the Skies of Poland (ANSA) - KONOTOPIE, 25 LUG - In a village in central Poland, a statue of the Virgin Mary soars above the fleecy July skies: while churches are emptying in this country with a long Catholic tradition, a tycoon has had Europe's tallest Marian monument erected there. Rising to a height of 55 meters, the white silhouette of concrete and steel beams stands, rigid and solemn, amid a sea of greenery and parking lots in the rural town of Konotopie, a three-hour drive northwest of Warsaw. Its dedication and blessing are scheduled for the Feast of the Assumption, August 15. For now, construction is still in full swing, under the dazed or fervent gaze of visitors. The Poles owe this gift to a multimillionaire compatriot, Roman Karkosik, who has spent some 100 million zlotys (23.1 million euros), according to local media. He himself lives nearby, in the neighboring town of Kikol, in a restored 18th-century palace across from the parish church. - Funding Devotion - For the faithful interviewed by AFP, devotion is priceless. "People come here (...) in search of faith," says Marek Gizinski, who traveled dozens of kilometers to pray. "And as with any miracle (...) you simply can't forget it—it's downright impossible to forget," he whispers, his gaze fixed on the Virgin Mary. Some local residents, however, believe that this giant statue is not the best way to represent the Catholic faith in a country already dotted with religious monuments, many of which commemorate the Polish Pope John Paul II. The country's main site of Marian devotion—a painting known as the "Black Madonna," located in the south—attracts between 3.5 and 5 million pilgrims each year. "Rather than for the Virgin, that money 'should have been invested in a hospital or an orphanage,'" laments a couple who came from the neighborhood. Entrepreneur Karkosik and his wife, among the wealthiest people in Poland, recently came to admire their creation—in a luxury car with a chauffeur. "Last Sunday, he came to visit the construction site from the back seat of his Maybach," jokes Andrzej, the site's caretaker. - A New Pilgrimage Site? - Local officials hope the project will bring economic benefits—unanticipated in this impoverished region. "I haven't heard any negative opinions (...) Everyone is generally satisfied," Renata Golebiewska, mayor of the neighboring town of Kikol, told AFP. In 2024, municipal tax revenue per capita in Kikol amounted to just 1,117 zlotys (258 euros), according to data from the Ministry of Finance—making it one of the least well-funded municipalities in the region. The statue in Konotopie is the second-tallest in the world after the "Mother of All Asia—Tower of Peace," completed in 2021 and standing 98.15 meters tall in Batangas City, Philippines, another deeply Catholic country. The Virgin Mary holds a special place in Poland's religious and national identity, where she has been venerated for centuries as the country's patroness and protector—even as the country experiences one of the fastest rates of secularization in the world. "We hope that this place will bear the fruits of a deeper return to the faith, or at least help people deepen their faith," says the parish priest, Marek Mrowczynski. Not entirely convinced, Wanda, who came with two friends, wonders above all how much the developers "are going to pocket." kw/ks/pop/jrt (ANSA). https://english.elpais.com/international.text: The fact that Spain is swimming against the tide on European immigration issues became more evident than ever on Friday, when several EU leaders led by the prime ministers of Denmark and Italy — Mette Frederiksen and Giorgia Meloni — strongly criticized the Spanish government’s decision earlier this year to grant legal status to potentially hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants. One of the toughest statements came from Frederiksen, who despite being one of the few social-democratic leaders in Europe, has opposing views to Spain’s socialist leader Pedro Sánchez when it comes to immigration. The Danish prime minister accused Sánchez of doing “almost the exact opposite” of what other EU member states are doing on this matter, and asked the European Commission, the union’s executive arm, to scrutinize Spain’s position. “I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” she said. “I believe this runs counter to the migration policy supported by a large majority in Europe today.” Frederiksen’s statements came after the by now traditional “migration breakfast” bringing together 18 member states as well as the European Commission, with a view to further restrict common immigration policies, among other things by accelerating the creation of third-country deportation centers. The Czech Republic’s prime minister, Andrej Babis, was also openly critical of Spain’s policy. “We see what is happening in Spain, how some politicians are capable of population replacement just to stay in their jobs and in government,” he said as he walked into the summit. And the Austrian chancellor, Christian Stocker, said it was a “bad sign” for Europe. According to diplomatic sources, several participants declared their intention to revisit the final conclusions of the document that will emerge from the summit in order to underscore their rejection of Spain’s plan to legalize undocumented migrants, which they see as having a “pull effect.” Many see evidence of this in the crisis experienced in Ceuta, a Spanish exclave city in northern Africa whose borders were stormed by around 80,000 people in just two days in late July. The city has yet to recover from the effects of the sudden influx, and thousands of migrants remain in makeshift camps and reception centers. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted in a letter before the summit that Europe’s policies are already achieving “substantial results,” including a 55% drop in illegal border crossings in the last two years, down to their lowest level since 2021. One source said ahead of the summit that even though the facts do not support the popular idea of uncontrolled immigration in Europe, “some countries are looking for a more emotional debate because they need it for domestic reasons,” citing a series of general elections coming up — beginning with Spain, which has called a snap election on November 29, to be followed by elections in France, Finland and others next year. Diplomatic sources said that the initiative to introduce amendments to the final conclusions — which must be adopted by consensus, which means Spain could block that section of it — was led by Denmark, Italy and Poland. The changes would involve underscoring that illegal immigration is something of concern to EU citizens, and that more work needs to be done to “reduce” the pull effect and any policies that might incentivize immigration to Europe. Those countries also want to explore ways to “encourage cooperation” among member states “when they enact national policies that affect others,” alluding once again to Spain’s plan to legalize migrants, which they feel could impact their own countries. https://hvg.hu/elet/20261124_tuz-utott-k.text: Nem ez az első tűzeset a sztár luxusbirtokán. Hétfőre virradóra tűz ütött ki Will Smith és Jada Pinkett Smith Los Angeles-i birtokán – írja a TMZ . A lángok egy raktárépületet érintettek a színész 42 millió dollár értékű rezidenciáján. A tűzoltók megfékezték a tüzet, senki sem sérült meg. Nem ez az első alkalom, hogy a színész birtokán tűz keletkezett, 2021-ben az alagsorban történt hasonló incidens – emlékeztet a Blikk . Egósimogatás, ujjakból formált szívecskék, szelfihegyek a rajongókkal – így szerette ismét a magyar fővárost és a rajongókat az amerikai színész-rapper a Budapest Parkban. Most nem a „Mocskos Fidesz!” szólt, hanem csak a „hey” meg a „ho” – és ez így volt jól. Koncertbeszámoló.

Photograph: Nozomi Imai Japan ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east Justin McCurry in Tokyo Thu 26 Nov 2026 00.16 EST Last modified on Thu 26 Nov 2026 00.19 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release. Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east. Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi , have denied the claims. Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying Read more His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China. The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war. In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”. “Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.” She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.” Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.” View image in fullscreen Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east. Photograph: Gribov Andrei/Alamy Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer. Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October. The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”. Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.” Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said. The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro. Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents. “They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.” Explore more on these topics Japan Russia Asia Pacific news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
